paragraphs: The following judgments concern marriage and family therapists' clinical and therapeutic practices. They do not predict hiring, licensing, qualification, or diagnostic outcomes, or replace clinical assessment.

The core work of marriage and family therapists is to diagnose and treat mental and emotional disorders within family and relationship systems: use questioning and observation to help clients identify feelings and behaviors, collect testing, interview, and observation information, diagnose mental and emotional disorders, develop individualized treatment plans, provide psychotherapy and family systems techniques for individuals, couples, and families, maintain case files containing progress notes and recommendations, and determine whether to provide counseling themselves or refer to medical, psychiatric, legal assistance, or other professionals.

Entirely fictional task package: provide fictional family relationship and counseling records, including 1 relationship and symptom description, 1 set of family-interaction observation points, and 1 risk clue to assess. Within 60 minutes, write an assessment approach, proposed treatment directions, circumstances requiring referral or escalation, and documentation and supervision points. This is solely an educational exercise. Do not use real client, patient, or clinical data or make any diagnosis from it.

Sample output and reflection: check whether safety and informed-consent boundaries were established first, observations were distinguished from assumptions, referral and supervision routes were stated, and documentation and confidentiality requirements were explained. Then ask yourself whether you can maintain neutrality and boundaries amid conflict and distress, identify risks beyond your competence or authorization and refer them, and willingly sustain clinical responsibility under supervision.

The fixed identity on this page corresponds to US ONet21-1013.00: assessing and treating mental / emotional disorders in marital and family systems and providing psychotherapy to individuals, couples, and families. Specific diagnostic, forensic assessment, and supervision tasks must remain within state licensing, competence, and task-specific authorization. US responsibilities do not automatically confer authority in China: psychological counselors in China may not provide psychotherapy or diagnose and treat mental disorders. Psychotherapy must take place in medical institutions; personnel specializing in psychotherapy may not diagnose mental disorders, prescribe medications, or provide surgical treatment.

entries: Inputs: client and family relationship and symptom information, interview and observation records, psychological measurement and assessment tools, treatment theories and family systems frameworks, referral and interdisciplinary information, case files and informed consent, and supervision and ethical requirements.

Checkable outputs: assessment and diagnostic conclusions, individualized treatment plans, treatment and progress notes, case files and recommendations, referral and consultation records, assessment statements for courts, and supervision and consultation records.

Complete workflow: establish safety and informed-consent boundaries → collect information and assess → develop diagnoses and treatment plans → provide treatment and document progress → judge referral or escalation needs → consult and receive supervision → assess outcomes and adjust.

paragraphs: Key judgments: safety risks for clients and family members, whether diagnosis and treatment fall within authorization and competence, whether medical or psychiatric referral is needed, confidentiality and informed-consent boundaries, and adequate documentation and supervision.

Environment and pace: primarily controlled indoor settings, with prolonged sitting and sustained face-to-face contact. Work requires frequent communication and documentation. Decision freedom is high but errors have serious consequences; time pressure and conflict are common. Schedules are often regular, with possible evening and weekend appointments.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 21-1013.00. Wage, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. Research conclusions do not establish mainland China's qualification, licensing, wage, or employment scope.

Check first: practice licensing and authorized scope, competence and supervision boundaries, informed consent and confidentiality requirements, client and family safety risks, referral and interdisciplinary collaboration routes, and documentation compliance requirements.

End-to-end work: establish safety and informed-consent boundaries, collect information and assess, develop diagnoses and treatment plans, treat and document progress, judge referral or escalation needs, consult and receive supervision, and assess outcomes. Do not begin treatment before safety or authorization conditions are confirmed. Refer any situation beyond competence or licensing scope.

Boundaries with adjacent roles: this page covers only marriage and family therapists. Clinical and counseling psychologists provide psychological assessment and treatment; school psychologists work in school settings; neuropsychologists provide neuropsychological assessment; substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors provide addiction counseling. Professional scopes of practice and statutory responsibilities are not interchangeable with this occupation.

Clinical and counseling psychologists typically hold a psychology doctorate or corresponding authorization and provide psychological assessment and treatment. Marriage and family therapists take a family and relationship systems approach. Their practice scopes and licensing systems differ.

School psychologists assess learning and behavior and support students in school settings; marriage and family therapists provide treatment in clinical and family settings. Service populations and authorizations differ.

Neuropsychologists emphasize assessment of the nervous system and cognitive functioning; marriage and family therapists emphasize relationship systems and emotional and behavioral treatment. Assessment tools and authorizations differ.

Substance abuse and behavioral disorder counselors emphasize addiction counseling and recovery support; marriage and family therapists emphasize family and relationship systems treatment. Addiction-related work requires collaboration or referral within licensing scope.
Boundaries of AI's impact on marriage and family therapists

Editorial task hypothesis: distinguish appointment management from generative AI, which may draft summaries of fictional material. No occupational adoption rates or job outcomes were obtained. Real session data requires checking confidentiality, consent, and organizational authorization, and people must still check records. AI does not independently diagnose, treat, or manage crises; cross-border practice requires checking the actual jurisdiction.

Occupational sources describe actual tasks and subjects: assessment and diagnosis, treatment plans, case files, referrals, and consultations. Tool capabilities, organizational adoption, and job outcomes are recorded separately; wage or employment data is not used as AI evidence.

Editorial comparison: organizing records or drafting materials may receive assistance, but there is no adoption-sequencing research. Family members' accounts, clinical risks, and the therapeutic relationship cannot be replaced or omitted by automated summaries.

Human control points: judge safety and crisis risks, develop diagnoses and treatment plans, treat within authorization and competence, maintain confidentiality and informed consent, receive supervision, and take responsibility for clinical consequences.

First conduct an offline exercise using entirely fictional family relationship and counseling records. Write assessment approaches, treatment directions, and referral and supervision points without relying on unverified automated advice or making diagnoses from it.
Editorial hypothesis: retrieval / drafting may receive assistance, but methods and permissions require validation. Ordinary appointment software does not demonstrate generative AI adoption.

Check clinical authority and confidentiality. Do not submit real sessions / cases to external AI without authorization. Qualified personnel must promptly assess and escalate suspected safety risks under organizational clinical procedures.

Insufficient evidence: this research did not obtain a Chinese occupational wage distribution safely matching 21-1013.00. Health and social work unit averages provide only employer context. They do not prove public data does not exist or that all family counseling belongs to a medical occupation. Verify Chinese and US practice authority separately.

Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, consider whether you can maintain neutrality and boundaries in relationship and conflict situations, systematically collect information and develop reviewable treatment plans, identify risks beyond competence or authorization and refer promptly, accept feedback under supervision and protect confidentiality, and tolerate clinical pressure where errors have serious consequences. Tools such as RIASEC can only propose hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.

Positive signals: listening and building trust, systematic assessment and documentation, risk recognition and referral, accepting supervision and feedback, and maintaining ethical and confidentiality boundaries.

Reasons for caution: difficulty maintaining neutrality and boundaries, making unverified judgments, unwillingness to accept supervision or disregard for confidentiality and ethics, or difficulty handling intense emotions and crisis pressure.

Trial activity: using entirely fictional family relationship and counseling records, rehearse assessment approaches, treatment directions, and referral and supervision points, and ask someone else to review them against the records.

The O*NET interest code is SI (Social–Investigative), emphasizing helping others and researching human behavior. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications, much less replace licensing.

General personality measures such as the Big Five do not provide job evidence for this occupation and can only support self-reflection. Continue checking through real assessment, treatment, and supervision experiences.
Type-based tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and can only support self-reflection.

Entry pathways and capability stages

ONet's new-hire education responses report 87% master's degree, 10% post-master's certificate, and 3% doctorate, separate from JobZone5 group preparation. BLS says US MFTs typically require a master's and every state requires licensing. Degrees and supervised experience do not automatically grant independent practice rights.

United States: a relevant master's from an accredited school, post-graduation supervised clinical experience for state-required hours, and a state-recognized examination, with specific state requirements checked separately. No exact Chinese occupational qualification match was established, but clear statutory boundaries exist: psychological counseling may not include psychotherapy or mental disorder diagnosis and treatment; psychotherapy is limited to medical institutions, and personnel specializing in psychotherapy may not diagnose, prescribe, or provide surgical treatment. A US MFT title or license cannot replace these authorities.

Education, training, certification, and licensing are different statuses. A master's degree or related certification does not automatically grant a practice license. Check licensing for independent diagnosis and treatment by US state and local competent authority. Do not practice without authorization.

Entry stage: practice assessment and interviewing, basic therapeutic techniques, case documentation, and referral procedures under licensed therapist supervision. Learn ethics, confidentiality, and licensing requirements and retain supervision records.

Evidence to show: use reviewable case records and supervisory feedback covering assessment approaches, treatment plans, referrals, and ethical considerations to demonstrate compliant clinical work under supervision.

Next step: check the target employer's service populations and supervision arrangements, state or local licensing and continuing education requirements, and confidentiality and documentation standards. Validate assessment, treatment, and collaboration abilities through real supervised cases.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience and licensing, workers may handle more complex cases, supervise others, develop treatment specialties, or move into organizational management, teaching and research, or private practice.

Tasks include helping clients identify feelings and behaviors, collecting information, diagnosing, developing treatment plans, maintaining case files, consulting and supervising, and providing court assessments in custody and visitation disputes. source_card.note: Check source scope, limitations, and statistical periods separately against the original evidence. Source usage notes: O*NET 21-1013.00 Marriage and Family Therapists (Summary): provides occupational identity, the official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 21-1013.00. Wage and employment data on that page cover this occupation. O*NET 21-1013.00 Tasks: provides tasks including diagnosing and treating mental and emotional disorders, developing treatment plans, maintaining case files, consultation and supervision, and providing court assessments. Task examples do not mean every position performs every task. O*NET 21-1013.00 Work Context: describes primarily controlled indoor work, sustained face-to-face contact, high decision freedom, serious consequences of errors, time pressure, conflict situations, and other contexts. US work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures. O*NET 21-1013.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS Display): 2025 BLS OEWS median wages for this occupation. This page does not display percentile wages. O*NET 21-1013.00 National Employment Trends: employment in 2024 and projections for growth and job openings in 2024—2034. Projections are not a hiring guarantee. Industries: 21-1013.00: the main industry on that page for 2024 is Health Care and Social Assistance. Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand. O*NET 21-1013.00 Education and Occupational Preparation: Job Zone 5; most positions require a master's degree, approximately 87%, while some require a post-master's certificate or doctorate. Education distribution does not establish mandatory requirements for every employer. Licenses & Certifications: 21-1013.00: O*NET provides state licensing and national certification lookup entry points. Certification and training do not equal authorization to practice or employer hiring requirements. BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook: Marriage and Family Therapists: explains that a master's degree is typically required and every state requires licensing to practice. These are US practice requirements and do not automatically map to other jurisdictions. Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025): assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level. An exposure index is not an adoption rate, job outcome, or hiring probability. Average Annual Wages of Employees in Urban Units in 2025: provides average annual wages by industry category for urban non-private and private units, including health and social work. Industry averages are not occupational medians and exclude individually owned businesses and freelancers. FermatMind Task Impact Scale for Marriage and Family Therapists: organizes potentially assisted tasks and human control points for task-level AI and fit discussions. An editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or licensing.
